title: PCAP → conversation → content
input: A supplied packet capture.
steps: Open the capture in Wireshark. Choose Statistics → Conversations; select a relevant peer pair and apply its conversation filter.
Select a packet, then Analyze → Follow → TCP Stream (or the matching supported protocol). Inspect both directions.
For transferred files, use File → Export Objects → the matching protocol; save only the relevant object to a new file.
expected: A readable exchange or exported object tied to a specific conversation.
fallback: For a large capture, use Zeek summaries to choose a stream; use TShark only when repeated field extraction is needed.
caveat: Encrypted payloads need supplied keys; missing packets may prevent reconstruction. Keep original captures.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

title: Disk image → partition → file
input: A raw disk image named `disk.img`; replace filenames and uppercase placeholders below.
steps: `mmls disk.img`: record the filesystem partition Start sector as OFFSET; for a filesystem-only image use OFFSET 0.
`fls -r -o OFFSET disk.img`: locate the desired path and record its metadata address as INODE.
`icat -o OFFSET disk.img INODE > recovered.bin`: write to a new output name, then inspect the recovered bytes.
expected: A path and metadata address, followed by the selected file contents.
fallback: If listing fails, check image type and offset first; use Autopsy for GUI inspection or PhotoRec only when filesystem metadata is unusable.
caveat: Sleuth Kit is recorded in WSL. Offsets are sectors; use the actual sector size if not 512 bytes. Deleted recovery may be incomplete; fls does not recurse into deleted directories.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

title: Memory image → process lead
input: A Windows memory image `memory.raw` and compatible locally cached symbols.
steps: From the installed Volatility 3 directory, run `python3 vol.py -f memory.raw windows.info` to check image and symbol recognition.
Run `python3 vol.py -f memory.raw windows.pstree` to find unusual process/parent relationships.
Run `python3 vol.py -f memory.raw windows.cmdline`; correlate arguments with the PID and parent you selected.
expected: A PID, parent and command line that identify the next artifact to inspect.
fallback: On symbol errors, resolve the matching symbols before trusting output. Use Volatility 2 only for a supported legacy image with its matching profile.
caveat: Volatility 3 runs in WSL and uses symbols, not Volatility 2 profiles. Prepare symbols before offline use; a missing process row does not prove absence.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

title: Image, audio or PDF → inspect the matching format
input: A local file; choose just the branch matching its format.
steps: PNG/BMP: run `exiftool -a -u -g1 image.png`; for PNG run `pngcheck -v image.png`. If pixel data is the clue, run `zsteg image.png` and validate meaningful hits.
Audio: open in Audacity, open the track menu and select Spectrogram. Adjust Spectrogram Settings frequency range and window size; inspect channels separately.
PDF: run `qpdf --list-attachments document.pdf` and `qpdf --show-pages document.pdf`; use a listed object number with `qpdf --show-object=OBJECT document.pdf`.
expected: Metadata/chunk findings, visible time-frequency patterns, or PDF attachment/object identifiers.
fallback: No meaningful result: revisit the format clue. zsteg is for PNG/BMP, not every image; a blank spectrogram may need different display settings.
caveat: Keep originals. ExifTool, zsteg and qpdf are WSL entries. pngcheck version is unknown; metadata and stego signatures need corroboration.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

toolkit.text: Use `python scripts/ctf.py inspect --file "image.jpg"` for bounded format evidence and selected image tags. A missing metadata tool produces a partial report; audio and PDF contents still need the approved format tools above.

title: Unknown executable → format and capabilities
input: A sample copied into a local analysis directory.
steps: Open the file in Detect It Easy and record format, architecture and probable packer.
For a supported executable named `sample.bin`, run `capa -v sample.bin`; record capability names and supporting addresses.
Open a relevant match location in the native-code route; inspect the surrounding function before accepting the capability claim.
expected: A format hypothesis and code locations worth investigating.
fallback: If packed or unsupported, select a matching extraction route; use FLOSS only when hidden strings are the specific blocker.
caveat: Signature and capability matches are leads, not observed execution. Static inspection does not require running the sample.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

title: Office or PDF → embedded code
input: An Office document `document.docm` or PDF `document.pdf`.
steps: Office: run `olevba document.docm`; inspect extracted VBA and the reported suspicious patterns.
PDF: from the installed Didier Stevens Suite directory, run `python3 pdfid.py document.pdf` to find noteworthy object types.
PDF: run `python3 pdf-parser.py document.pdf`; inspect references around flagged objects before selecting a stream for extraction.
expected: Macro source or PDF object references that explain the suspicious behavior.
fallback: No VBA is not a clean verdict: inspect embedded objects with the matching oletools utility; an encrypted or malformed file may block parsing.
caveat: Do not enable macros. PDF keyword counts alone are not proof; suite versions and script availability must match the installed copy.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

title: Identified bundle → extracted files
input: A file already identified as PyInstaller, Electron ASAR or UPX.
steps: PyInstaller: run `pyinstxtractor-ng sample.exe`; record the reported Python version and inspect the extracted directory.
Electron: run `asar list app.asar`, then `asar extract app.asar extracted-asar` into a new directory; inspect package.json and its entry point.
UPX: run `upx -t sample.exe`; if recognized, unpack to a new file with `upx -d -o unpacked.exe sample.exe`.
expected: Extracted source/bytecode or an unpacked executable for static inspection.
fallback: If the matching extractor fails, verify the format; modified packers and unsupported bytecode need manual reversing.
caveat: Choose one matching branch. Extraction does not execute or decompile the payload; Python version determines decompiler support. UPX approval is 4.2.4.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

title: HTTP request → one controlled change
input: A working request to the assigned challenge service.
steps: In Burp Proxy → HTTP history, select the request and choose Send to Repeater.
Send it unchanged; record status, response body and relevant cookies.
Change one parameter or header, send again, then restore the baseline. Compare content as well as status.
expected: A repeatable response difference attributable to one input.
fallback: If the baseline fails, refresh authentication/CSRF values and confirm the host before testing a hypothesis.
caveat: Burp Community is recorded in WSL; these steps need no Professional scanner. Keep requests and session tokens local.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

title: Missing endpoint → bounded discovery
input: An assigned base URL and a short local path list `paths.txt`; replace `https://challenge.example`.
steps: Request a unique nonexistent path in the browser; record its status, size and body to recognize wildcard responses.
Run `ffuf -w paths.txt -u https://challenge.example/FUZZ -rate 10 -t 1 -maxtime 60 -ac` against the assigned host.
Open promising hits manually and compare them with the nonexistent-path response.
expected: Candidate paths whose responses differ from the calibrated baseline.
fallback: Uniform responses may be wildcard pages or authentication redirects; recalibrate before increasing the list.
caveat: The rate/time bounds are starting limits, not event permission. Approved ffuf is a development build; confirm flags locally and locate SecLists data rather than assuming a path.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

title: Observed vulnerability → targeted test
input: A reproducible request plus evidence for a specific vulnerability class.
steps: Open the matching topic in the local PayloadsAllTheThings copy; check its prerequisites against the observed input and response.
In Repeater, change only that input using a relevant example; compare with the original request and a negative control.
Only for suspected SQL injection: save the valid raw request as `request.txt`, replace PARAM, then run `sqlmap -r request.txt -p PARAM --batch --level=1 --risk=1 --threads=1`.
expected: A reproducible class-specific response or sqlmap detection evidence for the selected parameter.
fallback: A negative or inconsistent result means revisit the hypothesis, encoding and session state; do not escalate to broad scanning by default.
caveat: References may name unapproved software. This SQL step detects; it does not request database dumping. Restrict testing to the assigned service.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

title: JWT → claims → server behavior
input: A token from a working request to the assigned application; replace TOKEN locally.
steps: From the installed jwt_tool directory, run `python3 jwt_tool.py TOKEN` to inspect header and claims.
Run `python3 jwt_tool.py TOKEN -T` to change one relevant claim using the local prompts; retain the original token.
Use Repeater to compare the original request, the modified token and a missing-token control; check actual protected content.
expected: A server-side acceptance or rejection tied to the changed token.
fallback: If every request fails, renew the baseline token and check expiry, audience and cookie placement before interpreting the test.
caveat: Decoding is not signature validation. A modified unsigned/invalid token should be rejected; acceptance must be confirmed from server behavior. Installed jwt_tool version is unknown.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

title: Native checker → validation logic
input: A native executable and its expected input format.
steps: In Ghidra, create a local project, import the executable, open it in CodeBrowser and accept analysis.
Use Search → for Strings to find a prompt or success/failure text; follow its references to the checking function.
Read the decompiler alongside the disassembly; rename input variables and record the comparison or transformation.
expected: A concrete input check with its data flow and success condition.
fallback: If static reasoning leaves a runtime question, use GDB in the matching native environment or x64dbg for Windows PE.
caveat: Ghidra and GDB are WSL entries. Decompilation can mislead; x32dbg is needed for 32-bit Windows targets. Run unknown code only in the intended isolated analysis environment.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

title: APK/DEX → validation method
input: A supplied APK or DEX, inspected without installation.
steps: Open the file in jadx-gui; inspect the manifest/package tree to locate the application entry points.
Search for a visible prompt or success/failure string; use Find Usage to reach the validation method.
Trace the input through comparisons and transforms; note any method JADX cannot reconstruct.
expected: A candidate validation method and the values it compares.
fallback: For failed methods or resource clues, decode a fresh directory with `apktool d app.apk -o decoded-app` and inspect smali/resources.
caveat: JADX cannot decompile every method correctly. Apktool is pinned to 2.7.0; do not copy newer-only flags.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

title: .NET assembly → C# and IL
input: A managed .NET executable or DLL.
steps: In dnSpyEx, choose File → Open and select the assembly.
Expand the assembly tree and locate the entry point or search for a prompt string; follow references to the validation method.
Read the C# view, then switch the language selector to IL where a condition or conversion is ambiguous.
expected: A validation method whose comparison and input handling can be explained.
fallback: If no managed assembly tree appears, verify the format and use the native-code route; obfuscated code may require inspecting IL.
caveat: dnSpyEx is installed on Windows and targets .NET; it is not a general native decompiler.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

title: Python, Java or JavaScript → source view
input: A PYC, JAR/class or JavaScript file; select the matching branch.
steps: PYC: run `pycdc module.pyc`; compare questionable output with `pycdas module.pyc`. Extract PyInstaller bundles first using the bundle route.
Java: create a new `java-out` directory, then run `java -jar /opt/tools/fernflower/build/libs/fernflower.jar app.jar java-out`; inspect the generated sources/archive.
JavaScript: run `js-beautify script.js` and follow the formatted validation logic without executing it.
expected: Readable source or disassembly for the input-validation path.
fallback: Unsupported Python opcodes require a version-compatible decompiler; formatted JavaScript may still need a matching deobfuscator.
caveat: Python support is version-dependent and reconstructed code can be incomplete. Fernflower uses the recorded local JAR path; JavaScript formatting does not remove semantic obfuscation.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

title: Image/date → metadata clue
input: A locally supplied original image `image.jpg`.
steps: Run `exiftool -a -u -g1 image.jpg` to retain duplicate tags and their groups.
Compare GPS, camera and date fields across groups; record any explicit time-zone offset and contradictory values.
Corroborate the selected clue with the supplied context or an independent public source; record its URL and date.
expected: A sourced location/date hypothesis with conflicts kept visible.
fallback: If metadata is absent, use visible clues and the public-source route; absence does not establish provenance.
caveat: ExifTool runs in WSL. Metadata may be forged, stripped or copied; a timestamp without an offset does not establish UTC.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

toolkit.text: Use `python scripts/ctf.py inspect --file "image.jpg"` to keep format evidence and selected tags together. No GPS is only a result for the queried tags; corroborate any clue using the approved route above.

title: Public phrase/page → source and date
input: A public phrase or page supplied by the challenge; internet access is required.
steps: In Chrome, search a distinctive public phrase in quotes, for example `"public phrase"`; add `site:example.org` only when a domain clue exists.
Open the source page rather than relying on the snippet; record the author, displayed date and surrounding context.
Find an independent source for the claim and retain both URLs; distinguish publication dates from the event date.
expected: A traceable claim with supporting sources and a stated date interpretation.
fallback: No exact match: shorten the quoted phrase or remove the domain restriction; archived or changed pages may remain unavailable.
caveat: Search only public clues, not private challenge files or secrets. Search rankings and page dates do not establish identity or truth.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

title: Public domain → candidate hostnames
input: A public domain explicitly supplied for OSINT; replace `example.org`. Internet access is required.
steps: Run `subfinder -d example.org -oJ -cs -o hosts.jsonl` to retain source provenance.
Inspect the JSONL records and shortlist hostnames relevant to the challenge clue.
Corroborate a candidate using its cited public source; record when the evidence was observed.
expected: Candidate hostnames and the public sources that reported them.
fallback: Zero results may mean missing provider keys or no public coverage; revisit the supplied domain and source availability.
caveat: Passive providers receive the queried public domain. Records may be stale; this is not a complete asset inventory or permission to probe discovered hosts.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

title: Encoded bytes → reversible transform
input: Encoded text or bytes and a local/offline CyberChef copy.
steps: Paste input into the local CyberChef input pane; choose From Base64 or From Hex only when the alphabet/format fits.
Inspect output bytes and text after this single layer. Undo it if the result contradicts the expected format.
Add another operation only when the output supports it; retain the recipe and verify the final structure or known content.
expected: A reproducible transformation from the supplied bytes to meaningful data.
fallback: If no layer is justified, Magic may propose candidates; validate each rather than accepting readable fragments.
caveat: Use a prepared offline copy, not a public upload workflow. Magic is heuristic; never share input-bearing recipe URLs.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

toolkit.text: For binary text, use `python scripts/ctf.py bits --file "bits.txt" --lines 2:3`; select only known payload rows. The toolkit also offers known-key file XOR with protected output. Keep CyberChef for short interactive recipes.

title: Hash/password → Hashcat recovery
input: A known-format hash file `hashes.txt` and local `candidates.txt`; replace MODE and GPU_IDS before running.
steps: Match the complete hash syntax and source format to Hashcat example hashes; select the numeric MODE. hashid guesses alone are insufficient.
Use the linked Hashcat cheatsheet to select devices, run a dictionary attempt, check optimized-kernel length limits and resume interrupted work.
Run `hashcat -m MODE hashes.txt --show`; validate any recovered value against the supplied artifact.
expected: Status shows the selected devices, speed and recovery count. Cracked means recovery succeeded; Exhausted means the tested candidates were consumed, not that the password is impossible to recover.
fallback: A parser/backend error is not an exhausted search. Check mode and device support first. If candidates are exhausted, use evidence to choose a better wordlist, an appropriate rule set (`-r RULE_FILE`) or a known-pattern mask; more rules or a larger search is not automatically more efficient. Archives/documents may need the matching installed John jumbo converter and format.
caveat: Check mode, backend and candidate-length limits locally. Keep password output private and preserve the installed wordlist. No match only rejects candidates that were actually tested.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

references.title: hashcat — Match hash formats and choose a recovery mode
Hashcat options: devices, optimized kernels and workload profiles

title: RSA → specific weakness → checked result
input: A textbook RSA public key `key.pub` and an evidenced weakness.
steps: Run `RsaCtfTool --dumpkey --key key.pub` to inspect n and e; compare them with the challenge clues.
If a small private exponent is the hypothesis, run `RsaCtfTool --publickey key.pub --attack wiener --private`; otherwise choose an attack only after checking its prerequisites.
For recovered factors, verify `p * q == n`; for a recovered plaintext integer m and ciphertext c, verify `pow(m, e, n) == c` in local Python.
expected: A recovered factor/key/plaintext checked against the original RSA parameters.
fallback: A failed attack does not disprove RSA. Use SageMath or crypto-attacks only when the supplied algebra matches a specific supported attack.
caveat: RsaCtfTool runs in WSL; launcher/flags may differ locally. Avoid all-attacks defaults and external factor services. The equality check assumes textbook RSA integers.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

title: Unknown artifact → identify → list/extract
input: A local file `artifact.bin`; use new output paths.
steps: Run `file artifact.bin`; use the content-based result to select the next parser.
For a supported archive, run `7z l artifact.bin` to inspect names and sizes before extraction.
Run `7z x artifact.bin -oextracted-artifact` into a new directory; inspect the relevant extracted file without executing it.
expected: A likely format and an archive listing or extracted artifact.
fallback: If identification is vague, inspect header bytes; use binwalk only when embedded signatures are the clue.
caveat: Signatures can mislead for truncated/polyglot data. Check available space before extraction; binwalk v2/v3 options differ.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

toolkit.text: Use `python scripts/ctf.py inspect --file "artifact.bin"` for a bounded report of format evidence and applicable ZIP/image metadata. It never extracts files; partial or unsupported results point back to the approved tools above.

title: Text, JSON or bytes → focused extraction
input: Local files; replace the example pattern/key and select the matching format.
steps: Text: run `rg -n -F "needle" evidence-dir`; add `--hidden` only when hidden files are relevant.
JSON: run `jq . data.json` to inspect structure, then `jq -r .key data.json` with the actual key/filter.

Binary: for a known four-byte little-endian unsigned field, run `python3 -c 'import struct; data = open("record.bin", "rb").read(4); print(struct.unpack("<I", data)[0])'`; adjust width/byte order only from the format specification.
expected: Matching lines, selected JSON values or a numeric field interpreted with explicit byte order.
fallback: No text match: check encoding and ignored/binary files; null JSON output may mean the wrong key. For a visible QR/barcode, use ZBar instead of text search.
caveat: jq and Python Windows-list entries run in WSL. Binary field width/endianness must come from the format; Python AI/ML libraries are excluded by the approval rules.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

references.title: ripgrep (rg) — Search text and selectively include hidden or binary files

toolkit.text: For selected binary-text rows, use `python scripts/ctf.py bits --file "rows.txt" --lines 2:3`. Invalid characters and incomplete groups stop conversion; inspect the source before changing grouping or line selection.

title: Challenge endpoint → protocol → interaction
input: An assigned HOST and PORT; replace these placeholders and restrict requests to that endpoint.
steps: Run `nmap -sV -p PORT HOST` to check the specified port and likely service.
For a plaintext TCP challenge, run `ncat HOST PORT`; for a specified TLS service use `ncat --ssl HOST PORT`.
Read the banner/prompt, send one protocol-appropriate input and record its response before automating.
expected: An observed protocol exchange that clarifies the challenge input/output.
fallback: No response: check VPN, host/port and TLS requirement. Use Impacket for an actual SMB task or socat only for a concrete transport need.
caveat: A service guess is not proof. Ncat connects here; it does not start a listener. Do not send arbitrary text to an identified binary protocol.
verification: Source-reviewed; not executed on competition machines.

title: Supplied Wi-Fi capture → offline candidate check
input: A supplied 802.11 capture and a local candidate wordlist; no live wireless activity.
steps: Inspect the capture in Wireshark for the target network and PMKID or EAPOL handshake evidence; record the BSSID/ESSID and any missing messages.

For a supported capture, choose a new nonexistent output path and run `hcxpcapngtool -o NEW_capture.22000 capture.pcapng`; inspect converter warnings and confirm the new records belong to this capture before selecting Hashcat mode 22000.
Run `hashcat -m 22000 -a 0 NEW_capture.22000 candidates.txt`, then `hashcat -m 22000 NEW_capture.22000 --show`; validate any result against the recorded network evidence.
expected: A supported authentication record and an explicit candidate result: a verified match or only the tested candidates exhausted.
fallback: No converted records may mean an incomplete handshake, a different security mode, or unsupported capture framing. Reinspect the capture before changing wordlists; a backend error is not exhaustion.
caveat: Only analyze supplied captures offline. Do not transmit deauthentication frames or use online upload helpers. hcxtools may append to an existing output file; a stale nonempty file is not conversion evidence.
verification: Source-reviewed against upstream hcxtools and Hashcat documentation; not run on competition machines.

title: EVTX → event lead → source record
input: Supplied Windows EVTX files and a question about an event, host or time window.
steps: Identify the relevant log channel and event ID from the clue. For PowerShell script-block event 4104, run `chainsaw search -t 'Event.System.EventID: =4104' ./logs` on a copied EVTX directory.
Inspect matching records in their source log; record file, Event ID, record ID, host, account, timestamp and time zone before correlating events.

If the question needs broader detection or ordering, use a prepared local Sigma rule/mapping with Chainsaw or the installed Hayabusa timeline command; confirm its version and rules before interpreting hits.
expected: A traceable event or ordered event set tied to source files and record identifiers, with a bounded interpretation.
fallback: No result: check whether the expected channel exists, whether parsing produced errors, and whether the selected time window or event ID is too narrow. Missing logs are not negative evidence.
caveat: Rule hits are leads, not a malware verdict. Normalize time zones and distinguish event time from file timestamps. Hayabusa command names differ across versions.
verification: Source-reviewed against Chainsaw and Hayabusa documentation; no EVTX fixture or competition-machine run.

title: Native crash → controlled primitive
input: A supplied native executable and its documented local input path; an assigned service is optional.
steps: Identify the executable format and architecture, then run `checksec --file=./challenge` for an ELF; record PIE, NX, canary and RELRO before interpreting a crash.

Reproduce the observed input under GDB. If input reaches a corrupted control value, use a bounded cyclic pattern and `cyclic_find` with the same subsequence size and byte order to establish an offset; confirm with a near miss.

Only after proving a usable primitive, inspect a specific gadget class with `ROPgadget --binary ./challenge --only 'pop|ret'` and verify address/load-base assumptions locally before adapting the TCP starter to an assigned service.
expected: A reproducible crash with a measured controlled value or a clear reason that this input has not established control.
fallback: If the process exits normally or a canary aborts first, trace the input path and failing check. Do not guess an offset or copy a gadget address into a different build.
caveat: Protection flags do not prove a vulnerability. PIE/ASLR, architecture, endianness and remote library versions affect addresses; keep unknown executables in the intended isolated runtime.
verification: Source-reviewed against checksec, pwntools and ROPgadget references; no exploit or competition-machine run.

title: ZipCrypto ZIP → known plaintext → checked recovery
input: A supplied ZipCrypto archive and exact known bytes for one member; use new output filenames.
steps: Run `7z l -slt archive.zip`; identify the member, encryption method and compression method. Continue with bkcrack only for ZipCrypto and known bytes of its encrypted compressed stream.

Prepare at least 11 exact supplied plaintext bytes, including eight contiguous; bkcrack adds one inferred ZIP header check byte for archive input. Run `bkcrack -C archive.zip -c MEMBER -p known.bin` against the matching member.

If internal keys are recovered, use `bkcrack -C archive.zip -c MEMBER -k KEY1 KEY2 KEY3 -d NEW_member` for the selected member and validate its bytes. Use `-D NEW_archive.zip` and `7z t` only when all archive members share the same keys.
expected: Recovered internal keys and a structurally valid decrypted member, or a clear failed precondition; the original password need not be recovered.
fallback: ZIP AES is outside this attack. For a deflated member, original file-header bytes may not match the compressed stream; revisit that assumption instead of extending a blind search.
caveat: The tutorial's easy case is stored data. A deflated member's decrypted bytes still need decompression. Do not treat guessed bytes or reported keys as verified until the selected member passes an independent check.
verification: Source-reviewed against the bkcrack 1.8.1 tutorial; no local bkcrack run or competition-machine check.

title: Registry hive → key evidence → corroboration
input: A copied Windows registry hive and, when supplied, its transaction logs.
steps: Identify whether the source is SYSTEM, SOFTWARE, SAM, SECURITY or a user hive; keep its path and any LOG1/LOG2 companions with a working copy.

From the installed RegRipper directory, use `rip.pl -l` to choose a plugin, then run `rip.pl -r HIVE -p PLUGIN` on the copied hive; record the plugin, source hive, key/value and displayed last-write time.
Check the decisive value in a second approved registry view or related artifact and resolve the timestamp's time basis before drawing a timeline conclusion.
expected: A specific key/value or other registry artifact tied to its hive, plugin and corroborating evidence.
fallback: If the hive is dirty or a recent value is missing, account for transaction logs; RegRipper does not replay them automatically. A plugin mismatch or missing hive is not absence of the artifact.
caveat: Run on copies. Last-write time belongs to a key and does not identify the actor or prove that every value changed then; keep log replay and time-zone assumptions explicit.
verification: Source-reviewed against RegRipper 3.0 CLI; no Windows hive or competition-machine run.

references.title: RegRipper 3.0 CLI syntax and transaction-log limit

title: SQLite + WAL → schema → selected records
input: A local SQLite database, with any -wal and -shm sidecars from the same snapshot.
steps: Preserve a coherent copy of the database and its matching -wal/-shm files in a working directory; record if a sidecar is missing or the source was live during collection.
Run `sqlite3 -readonly COPY.db '.tables'`, then `sqlite3 -readonly COPY.db '.schema TABLE'`; query only the relevant rows with an explicit order and inspect timestamp units before converting dates.
Cross-check a decisive row against the source application context or a second read-only view; if this is browser history, use Hindsight only when its parser supports the supplied profile version.
expected: A table, selected row and interpreted time field with database and sidecar provenance.
fallback: A read-only WAL open can fail when sidecars or directory permissions are unsuitable. Copy the complete set into a writable analysis directory; do not infer empty data from a missing WAL or parser error.
caveat: The CLI opens the database read-only but may create working shared-memory files. Do not use Write Changes on evidence or treat a schema field name as proof of its time epoch.
verification: SQLite -readonly with copied DB/WAL/SHM locally checked on a synthetic database; competition-machine and browser-profile behavior unverified.

references.title: SQLite CLI schema and read-only mode

title: Suspected SQL input → paired response check
input: A working request to an assigned challenge endpoint and one suspected query parameter.
steps: Replay the unchanged request twice in Burp Repeater; record status, relevant body content, cookies and any server-side state before editing the suspected parameter.
Use one syntax probe and a matched true/false condition appropriate to the observed input type and quoting; compare both with the unchanged request and a non-SQL negative control.

Only after a repeatable SQL-specific difference, consult the matching local PayloadsAllTheThings topic or use a narrowly configured approved sqlmap test for that request and parameter; verify any result in the application.
expected: A stable response or state difference explained by the paired SQL condition, or an explicit inconclusive result.
fallback: Generic errors, reflections, cache changes, validation failures and expired sessions can mimic a signal. Restore the baseline and choose a control that separates those causes.
caveat: SQL syntax varies by database and query position. Avoid broad automation or write-changing statements without challenge evidence and scope; a single quote error alone is not a SQLi finding.
verification: Source-reviewed against PortSwigger SQL injection and Repeater guidance; no challenge service tested.

title: URL input → server-side fetch evidence
input: An assigned application with a URL-like input and a challenge-provided benign destination or request log.
steps: Replay the application's normal URL-input request unchanged and determine whether the browser redirects, the server fetches content, or an asynchronous job handles it.

In Repeater, change only the URL to an authorized benign destination with a unique marker, then use a malformed or blocked destination as a control; inspect response content and any available challenge-provided request log.
Only when server-originated fetching is evidenced, test the specific URL parser or trust boundary suggested by the challenge and confirm the observed effect at the authorized destination.
expected: A marker or log entry tied to a server-originated request, separated from a client redirect or reflected URL.
fallback: A changed status, echoed URL or browser navigation alone does not establish SSRF. Check caching, asynchronous timing, redirects and whether the destination is reachable from the server.
caveat: Keep destinations within the assigned challenge scope. Do not send challenge content to an external callback or probe arbitrary internal addresses based only on a URL field.
verification: Source-reviewed against PortSwigger SSRF and Repeater guidance; no live endpoint tested.

title: Object reference → authorization comparison
input: Two permitted principals with objects whose ownership is known from the challenge.
steps: Record a working request for an object owned by principal A and a comparable object owned by principal B; keep their sessions separate and save a nonexistent-object control.
In Repeater, send A's object reference under B's authenticated session while keeping other request fields stable; compare with B's own-object and nonexistent-object responses.
Inspect the actual returned object data or state change and the challenge's intended access rule before calling the difference an authorization bypass.
expected: A demonstrated cross-principal access to data or action that the intended rule forbids, or a checked rejection.
fallback: Shared/public objects, generic 200 pages, cache hits, missing CSRF values or no second principal make the result inconclusive. Do not enumerate object IDs to replace missing ownership evidence.
caveat: Keep tokens private, avoid cross-user state changes without a challenge need, and distinguish read access from write authorization.
verification: Source-reviewed against PortSwigger IDOR/access-control guidance; no live challenge tested.

title: File path input → verified outside-root read
input: An assigned file-serving request, its intended root, one allowed file, and a permitted benign outside-root file with independently known bytes.
steps: Save the working file request and repeat it unchanged in Burp Repeater; compare the allowed file's raw response body bytes with one missing-file control, recording exact request encoding, session and intended serving root.

Change only the file input to one relative path reaching a known benign file outside that root. Preserve byte-exact encoding of untouched query fields, record the selected value's encoding, and keep requests bounded to the assigned service.

Compare the returned raw response body bytes with the file's independently known bytes, then check its location against the intended root and the missing-file response before treating the result as a cross-boundary read.
expected: Exact independently known outside-root file bytes from the selected endpoint, or an explicit inconclusive result.
fallback: A reflected path, generic 200, redirect, error, or WEB05 marker lead does not prove a file read. If the outside file or its bytes are unknown, or a wrapper transforms the response, record a hypothesis until a reliable byte comparison is possible.
caveat: Use only a permitted benign file on the assigned service; do not request unrelated private files or spray paths. A readable outside file still needs a known intended root and access rule before it demonstrates a flaw.
verification: OWASP and PortSwigger source-reviewed; positive, reflected-path and generic-200 controls exercised on a disposable loopback fixture. No live challenge or competition machine tested.

title: XOR or reused stream → aligned bytes → checked plaintext
input: Two byte strings with evidence of the same XOR stream, or one ciphertext with a known plaintext segment.
steps: Decode the inputs to raw bytes and record their lengths and offsets. For two matching keystream positions, compute C1 XOR C2 = P1 XOR P2; this relation alone does not reveal either plaintext.

Use an independently known plaintext segment to derive only its aligned keystream bytes, then apply those bytes at the matching positions. Use the approved CyberChef XOR operation or the local known-key XOR helper only when the key and repetition pattern are established.

Reapply derived bytes as an arithmetic sanity check, then require independent known-plaintext, strong format, or checker evidence before accepting any proposed message; the XOR round trip alone proves nothing about keystream reuse.
expected: A bounded plaintext segment supported by independent evidence and consistent byte equations, with unknown positions left unknown.
fallback: If lengths, start offsets, or counter blocks differ, alignment may be wrong. A printable guess or shared cipher name is not evidence that the same keystream bytes were used.
caveat: Do not repeat a short derived segment unless repeating-key XOR is evidenced. CTR requires unique counter blocks under a key; nonce reuse alone does not prove every position aligns.
verification: Source-reviewed against NIST CTR requirements and Cryptopals fixed-nonce example; no competition-machine check.

title: Declared AES mode → required inputs → verified result
input: A ciphertext plus declared AES mode, key, and the mode-specific IV/nonce, tag, AAD or padding details.
steps: Record whether the ciphertext/key fields are hex, Base64 or raw bytes. For GCM require nonce, tag and any AAD; for CBC require the IV and padding rule; for CTR require the full initial counter block and its layout.
Run a bounded local transform with the matching approved tool or the documented `symmetric_parameters` helper. Do not use `openssl enc` for GCM; it does not support authenticated modes.

Require GCM tag verification before accepting its plaintext. For CBC/CTR, treat output as a candidate until an independent MAC, strong source-format check, known plaintext, or the challenge's checker supports it; forward encryption with the same parameters is only an implementation consistency check.
expected: Authenticated plaintext for a matching GCM record, or explicitly tentative CBC/CTR bytes with an independent check.
fallback: A missing tag, AAD, IV, counter layout, or wrong representation leaves the transform unverified. Recheck the stated parameters before trying unrelated modes.
caveat: Counter/IV reuse and mode confusion can invalidate assumptions. A CBC padding check is not proof that the supplied key or plaintext is correct.
verification: Source-reviewed against NIST mode specifications and OpenSSL enc documentation; local symmetric helper has synthetic GCM/CBC/CTR tests, not event-machine validation.

title: CBC padding oracle → calibrated response → candidate plaintext
input: An authorized endpoint accepting a supplied CBC ciphertext, with its IV layout and full block size known or evidenced.
steps: On a copied sample, preserve the original ciphertext and response. Change one byte in the IV or preceding block while keeping length, encoding, session and other fields fixed; repeat baseline and mutations to identify a stable padding-specific error distinct from a valid-padding response.

Check a nonpadding control and malformed-length response. Repeat the valid/invalid comparison with just the previous block plus target block in the exact field the tool would replace; stop if length, IV layout, MAC, AEAD tag, generic error, rate limit or authentication gates hide the padding result.

Only when the endpoint accepts that two-block payload in one injection field, use padding-oracle-attacker with the exact representation and observed error marker, `-c 1` and `--disable-cache`; bound requests and stop if response classes drift. Compare recovered bytes with independent known plaintext, source format, MAC or checker evidence.
expected: A repeatable oracle classification and tentative recovered bytes with independent validation, or no distinguishable padding signal under the tested conditions.
fallback: If valid and changed ciphertexts produce the same response, first check IV placement, encoding and session continuity. A separate IV field or fixed-length ciphertext may require a different method; do not feed a mismatched layout to this CLI.
caveat: CBC/PKCS#7-style padding and editable previous-block bytes are prerequisites. One altered byte may accidentally leave valid padding, so use repeated controls. Default tool concurrency is 128 and its cache can retain responses; use conservative explicit options and keep challenge data private.
verification: Source-reviewed and locally exercised with isolated padding-oracle-attacker 0.2.4 against a benign CBC oracle: recovered bytes matched known plaintext. A generic-response control produced false output, so response classes and independent validation remain required. Competition-machine behavior is unverified.

title: Git history → deleted or changed artifact
input: A supplied local Git repository or its copied directory; no remote fetch is needed.
steps: Preserve the repository, then run `git -C REPO status --short` and `git -C REPO log --all --oneline --decorate` to record available refs and distinguish tracked history from untracked working files.

For an evidenced path, run `git -C REPO log --all --follow --oneline -- PATH`; choose a commit where the file exists and inspect only that blob with `git -C REPO show COMMIT:PATH`. For a deletion, identify the relevant parent commit explicitly.

Relate the exact commit, path and blob bytes to the challenge clue. If the approved Gitleaks tool reports a possible secret, treat it as a lead and verify only the relevant history without sharing the value.
expected: A specific source commit and path containing the relevant bytes or a documented missing-history limit.
fallback: An empty result may reflect a shallow/incomplete repository, a renamed path, an untracked file, or a missing ref. Recheck supplied objects and paths before concluding the data never existed.
caveat: Do not fetch remotes or print entire histories by default. `--follow` is a single-path aid and may not explain complex merges; a historical credential or scanner hit is not proof that it is still valid.
verification: Source-reviewed against Git log/show and Gitleaks documentation; locally checked on a synthetic repository with a deleted file.

references.title: Git log path and history options

title: Browser profile → selected visit timeline
input: A coherent local copy of a Chrome/Chromium or Firefox profile, including History or places.sqlite and matching WAL/SHM sidecars when present.
steps: Record browser/profile path and version; work on a copy. If installed Hindsight help lists `--only`, run `hindsight.py -i PROFILE_DIR -o PRIVATE_OUT --only history` and use `-b Firefox` only when profile detection needs the override.

Inspect the parser status, skipped artifacts, selected visit row and time zone. If selective parsing is unavailable, inspect the copied History or places.sqlite schema with `sqlite3 -readonly` and use the browser-specific read-only query in the bundled workflow.

Cross-check a decisive visit against its exact source database row and independent context such as a known local server log. Keep the raw timestamp, UTC interpretation, source file and parser version together.
expected: A selected visit record with source-profile and time provenance, or a documented parser/schema limit.
fallback: A missing row may reflect absent WAL sidecars, a different profile, unsupported parser/schema, a filtered artifact, or a wrong time basis. An empty report alone cannot prove the visit never happened.
caveat: Hindsight can parse cookies and saved passwords by default; require a supported selective filter or use SQLite instead, and keep private output local. A stored visit does not identify the human actor. Download analysis needs its own source-specific check.
verification: Hindsight CLI and browser schemas source-reviewed; local synthetic SQLite query exercised; Hindsight and competition-profile execution unverified.

title: iOS plist → named field path and context
input: A supplied accessible XML or binary plist with its source path and app/container context; a full extracted filesystem is optional.
steps: Preserve a copy and record its path and hash. Use approved Python `plistlib.load` on a named plist and inspect a specific key path and value type; the bundled workflow gives a bounded local snippet for both XML and binary formats.

If a complete extracted filesystem is supplied and iLEAPP is available, check its local help, create a private output directory, then run `ileapp -t fs -i EXTRACTION_DIR -o PRIVATE_OUT`; keep parser/module version and any errors.
Tie the chosen key, value type and timestamp basis to the source plist and independent app or case context. Treat a parser report as a lead, not as proof of a different file or time epoch.
expected: A named key path/value with original plist path, format, type, and justified meaning; or a documented unsupported/absent state.
fallback: Encrypted or incomplete backups, unsupported keyed archives, malformed plists and unavailable iLEAPP leave the question open. Inspect the raw copied file and choose another supported view without assuming missing data.
caveat: Do not infer a universal timestamp epoch from a numeric plist field; confirm the field definition before conversion. Keep potentially private report content out of shared notes.
verification: Python plistlib XML/binary and malformed controls checked locally on synthetic files; iLEAPP command source-reviewed only, not installed in this WSL environment.

title: Reflected input → browser output context
input: A stable request to an assigned application that renders one controlled value in an HTML response.
steps: Replay the working request unchanged twice in approved Burp Repeater, then change one input to a unique inert marker. Keep the raw response status, Content-Type, response bytes and nearby HTML syntax.

Use Burp Repeater’s Show response in browser on the selected response; open its unique URL in Burp’s browser or Chrome configured through Burp. Compare the raw response, parsed DOM and console/CSP messages without issuing a new main request; watch for separate asset requests.

If a controlled execution check is justified, use only a local DOM marker with no network or secret access. Compare the changed request with baseline and negative controls; record whether code executed, merely appeared as text/markup, or was blocked by policy.
expected: A reproducible output context and browser observation, with a source request and controls; a reflected string alone is not an execution finding.
fallback: A missing or changed marker may be due to encoding, sanitization, redirect, cache, session/CSRF expiry, or client-side rendering. Re-establish the same response and sink before changing the hypothesis.
caveat: Use only the assigned service and harmless local effects; no credential reads, external callbacks, or broad payload spraying. CSP blocking an inline test is a specific observation, not proof that all contexts are safe.
verification: OWASP, MDN and Burp source-reviewed; locally exercised encoded text, unblocked execution and CSP-blocked markup on a synthetic loopback page; no live challenge tested.

title: Browser session → cross-site state change
input: A permitted reversible, form-compatible GET/POST action in an assigned app, your own authenticated browser session, and an independent state readout.
steps: Record the state before testing. Perform one legitimate same-site action in Chrome and capture its method, Content-Type, fields, cookie attributes, CSRF token and response in Burp; use a unique reversible marker so the resulting state is identifiable.

Adapt the bundled one-click cross-site form on a different local site. In the same disposable browser session, match the form-supported method and encoding, then send it once with only fields available to that outside site; capture the actual Cookie, Origin and Sec-Fetch-Site headers, and run a nearby unauthenticated or invalid-token control after restoring state or choosing a fresh marker.

Read the application state again through a fresh independent request. Tie any state delta to the exact browser request and compare it with the baseline and negative control before calling the result a candidate.
expected: An independently observed state delta with request/session provenance, or a documented blocked or inconclusive result.
fallback: No state change can reflect SameSite cookie rules, a CSRF token, Origin/Fetch Metadata validation, expired session, wrong request shape, or an unobservable state. Recheck the browser request and readout; status or reflection alone cannot decide.
caveat: Only use your own permitted account and a reversible action. A plain form supports GET/POST and form encodings, not PUT/PATCH/DELETE or JSON/custom headers; cross-origin and cross-site are different boundaries, and a CORS read failure does not prove the form was blocked.
verification: Source-reviewed against OWASP/MDN; six benign two-origin HTTPS browser cases locally checked in Chrome 148, including Lax/None cookie and CSRF-token controls. No live challenge or competition-machine test.

title: Android app extraction → one preference key
input: A supplied accessible app-data extraction with a named SharedPreferences XML file and any matching .bak, its app package/user context and original path; an APK alone is insufficient.
steps: Preserve the source and work on a copy. Record Android user, app package, original XML/.bak paths and hashes; if a complete extraction and approved ALEAPP are available, check local help and parse the copied extraction into a precreated private output directory.

For one evidenced key, run the bundled bounded Python snippet separately on the copied XML and any matching .bak; record the stored type and a short local value preview from each without dumping all preferences.

Compare the key and meaning with app code/configuration, a second source artifact or a known case observation. Treat ALEAPP output as a lead and confirm any decisive value against the copied source file.
expected: One named key/value/type tied to its source app, Android user, XML/backup path and independent context; or a documented parser/input limit.
fallback: A missing key can reflect another user, app version, DataStore or another storage mechanism, incomplete/encrypted extraction, conflicting XML/.bak, unsupported type/encoding or malformed XML, or unavailable ALEAPP. Do not infer that the app never held the value.
caveat: The snippet previews only a small copied UTF-8 SharedPreferences XML file and one string, boolean, or decimal int/long key; it rejects DTDs and large input. Other valid Android types or encodings need another parser. A backup can supersede the main XML when Android next loads preferences. Numeric fields need app-specific units and epoch before time conversion. Keep private values out of shared notes.
verification: Android/ALEAPP/Python documentation source-reviewed; local synthetic string/boolean/int/long bounds, XML/.bak disagreement, missing, malformed, UTF-16 DTD, size, symlink and FIFO controls passed. ALEAPP and competition-machine execution unverified.

title: Android Preferences DataStore → one typed key
input: A supplied accessible app-data extraction containing a copied files/datastore/*.preferences_pb file, exact key, app package/user context and original path; an APK alone is insufficient.
steps: Preserve the original extraction; record Android user, app package, source path and hash before working on a copy. Confirm this is Preferences DataStore rather than an app-defined Proto DataStore file.

Use the bundled bounded Python reader to select one exact key from the copied .preferences_pb file. It supports boolean, int32, int64 and string values, validates the full map, and reports unsupported selected types or malformed input instead of silently guessing.

Keep the selected value private and relate its stored type and meaning to independent app code, configuration, log or case evidence. Treat an ALEAPP report as a lead until its source file and parser version are confirmed.
expected: One named stored scalar type/value tied to its package, Android user, exact file and independent context, or a documented format/parser limit.
fallback: A missing key in one copy does not prove the app never held it: check extraction completeness, app/user/version, alternate files, and whether the app instead uses SharedPreferences XML or Proto DataStore.
caveat: The standard-library reader accepts only a regular .preferences_pb copy up to 1 MiB and rejects duplicate/malformed records. Selected float, double, string-set and byte-array values need another parser; app-defined Proto DataStore needs that app's schema. Numeric units and time epochs are app-specific.
verification: AndroidX schema and Android documentation source-reviewed; benign official-proto values matched the local bounded reader, with mixed-type, missing-key, duplicate, truncation, unsupported-type, size, symlink and FIFO controls. ALEAPP, Android runtime and competition machines untested.
